title: How Nvidia Uses Its Soft Power to Influence Customers and Shape Policy
summary: Last month, OpenAI Senior Research Scientist Noam Brown posted a link in a company Slack channel to a news story about OpenAI’s changing stance on advanced chip sales to China and asked a blunt question: “What is our policy on chip exports?” OpenAI policy leaders responded on Slack by citing past company posts, such as a safety blueprint on frontier AI published in June, that supported general chip export controls but did not address China specifically. They also directed staffers to speak to members of the global affairs team working on new export control policies, rather than discussing it on Slack. Chip restrictions are a delicate topic at the company. Over the past year, OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the issue of chip export controls for China because OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, have expressed concern that doing so will alienate chipmaker Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, according to people with knowledge of the company’s strategy. Last year, as Congress turned its attention to export control legislation, a senior OpenAI policy staffer privately said OpenAI was not as vocal on chip export controls as it had been under the Biden administration because it feared antagonizing Huang and Nvidia, according to a staffer on Capitol Hill.

title: Salesforce’s M&A Blitz Reflects Broader Deal Rush
summary: Anyone with an interest in tech will be glued to the TV or social media tonight, monitoring the midterm elections. As my colleague Shane Burke writes below, more than 20 candidates in state governor races support a moratorium on data center development. There’s also the California billionaire tax, Proposition 40, to track. But for those in tech fretting about the results, remember this: Nothing that happens tonight will change the relaxed antitrust regime we’ve got right now. That’s thanks to the Trump administration, not Congress. And that means companies have got two more years to get deals done before the antitrust climate could change. That's why the tech deal scene lately has resembled that old “ Supermarket Sweep ” TV game show where contestants have a limited amount of time to grab stuff off the shelves in a supermarket. We’ve seen deals such as Marvell and Lumentum on Monday, DoorDash and Instacart last week, Fox and Roku in June and many others. It’s not just tech, either (think Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery). Overall, deals worth $2.6 trillion have been announced so far this year, according to Dealogic, 66% more than at this time last year.

title: Should OpenAI Be Afraid of Jensen Huang?
summary: News flash: A lot of people in Silicon Valley are afraid of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . They have understandable reasons to be fearful, as Leo, Phoebe and I detailed in our story this morning. The chipmaker has a lot of money and influence to throw around, since Huang has the ear of several top government officials, including President Trump . More importantly for model developers like OpenAI , Nvidia controls the flow of AI chips they need to develop and run today’s most advanced models. It’s been hard enough for AI developers to get access to those chips, so it makes sense that the companies would want to avoid anything that might upset Huang. This has led to a situation where OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the current debate over chip sales to China for fear of alienating Nvidia and Huang, which generates plenty of revenue from Chinese companies and wants access to the Chinese market itself. (Nvidia isn’t allowed to sell its most advanced tech directly to that market, but Chinese firms like ByteDance and DeepSeek still find a way to access the chips outside China’s borders or through smuggled hardware .)

title: AI Agenda Live: EY Consulting on Bringing AI ROI to your P&L
summary: The capabilities AI can bring to companies seem limitless. So do AI token bills, which have skyrocketed, pressuring CFOs and boards to show that such spending can actually boost revenue or profits. Dan Diasio, EY Global AI Leader and Consulting CTO , has led teams advising the world’s largest companies on their AI transformations. The Information Editor-in-Chief Jessica Lessin sat down with Diasio to discuss why productivity gains from AI aren’t automatically showing up as financial returns and what has to change for them to do so. From enthusiasm to ROI According to Diasio, rising token costs haven’t dampened enterprise enthusiasm for AI. But enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to move profit margins. To underscore this point, he referred to two surveys suggesting that many organizations believe AI is paying off, but few can yet trace those returns in their financial results. The first, conducted by The Information , found that a third of organizations reported getting a return from AI that was a multiple of what they spend on it. The second, an EY survey conducted as part of the EY CEO Imperative Series , found that only 11% of CEOs say their companies link AI impact to financial reporting and review it regularly at the senior management level. “There’s value in increasing productivity, and there’s the value organizations need to be able to prove in their [profit and loss statement], and those are two different things,” Diasio said. “Many organizations I talk to would say AI is significantly increasing productivity. But when the CFO looks at the investment, that productivity needs to translate into two things: Are we making more revenue, and are we taking costs out of the organization?” Thinking beyond use cases What this means is that business leaders have to devise more concrete plans for AI  than they did in past cycles. “I’m seeing this big pivot from ‘let’s go identify some use cases’ to using AI to drive business transformation,” he said. To illustrate the point, Diasio described how a consumer products company could use AI to cut the time from product idea to market from 18 months to three, a move that would drive revenue by bringing more products to market faster. “That’s the sort of change that enterprises need to see to be all in,” he said. The agent handoff As part of that transformation, organizations are rethinking the relationship between human employees and so-called AI agents and, in many cases, finding unique ways to use agents to create value. Diasio pointed to banks, which have started using agents to assist financial advisors and streamline back-office work. The real value, he said, is in how those AI-assisted touch points build the bank’s relationships with clients and hopefully pay off by  helping it generate more revenue. “They’re using a lot of these AI capabilities not as a way of reducing costs, but of building brand,” he said of the banks. Starting fresh Ultimately, making AI’s payoff visible in financial results is going to require organizations to think of AI less as a technology rollout and more as a driver of measurable results. That means redesigning whole business functions from the ground up, not just automating pieces of them. “Fast-forward 12 months and companies are going to start thinking about new ways to run their business in parts,” he said. “That means doing the hard thing: addressing the processes that need to be entirely rebuilt.” That’s a harder path than simply adopting new tools, he said, but it’s the one that actually shows up on the P&L.
